title: Operational Security (OpSec)
summary: Operational security, usually shortened to OpSec, is the practice of controlling the observable traces an activity produces so that they do not reveal capability, intent, identity or infrastructure to an observer. The classic process has five steps: identify the information that must not be disclosed, analyse who is collecting against it, analyse the weaknesses in how the activity is conducted, assess the risk each weakness creates, and apply countermeasures in proportion. In security work the concept applies in two directions. On the adversarial side it explains why intrusions are often quiet, consistent and patient: infrastructure is separated by purpose, personas are maintained consistently across channels, timing follows the target's working rhythm, and released artefacts are sanitised of metadata before use. Understanding that discipline is directly useful to defenders, because every trace an intruder must suppress is a trace worth monitoring, and every inconsistency in a persona or infrastructure set becomes a pivot for attribution at a stated confidence level. On the defensive side, OpSec governs incident response itself: communications move off potentially compromised channels, actions that would alert an intruder are delayed until containment is ready, and information about the investigation is shared strictly on a need-to-know basis. Poor OpSec in either direction produces preventable loss, whether that is a burned capability or an intruder who destroys evidence after noticing that they have been detected.
objectives: You will be able to apply the five-step OpSec process to a security activity and its observable traces.
You will be able to identify which traces an intruder must suppress and convert them into monitoring requirements.
You will be able to explain how inconsistencies in infrastructure and persona support attribution at a stated confidence level.
You will be able to plan incident response communications that do not alert an active intruder.
You will be able to judge when operational silence harms an investigation more than it helps.
